note: Defensive detection patterns for the LUQI financial-literacy skill. Bump `version` on any pattern change; this file is the versioned source of truth (UNIFY-13).

patterns.name: Ponzi / pyramid scheme
patterns.description: Promises of high, fixed, or 'guaranteed' returns — especially monthly percentages or referral-based earnings. Paying old investors with new investors' money.
patterns.sa_example: Mirror Trading International (MTI) and Africrypt — two of the largest crypto Ponzi collapses in history — were South African. Both promised steady monthly returns.
patterns.advice: No legitimate investment guarantees returns. If returns depend on recruiting others, it is a pyramid scheme — illegal under the Consumer Protection Act. Check FSCA registration before investing a single rand.

patterns.name: Advance-fee fraud (419)
patterns.description: You are told money is waiting (prize, inheritance, loan, refund) but you must first pay a fee to 'release' it. The money does not exist.
patterns.sa_example: SMS or email claiming you won a lottery you never entered, or that an 'R500 000 inheritance' needs a R2 000 'clearance fee'.
patterns.advice: Real institutions deduct fees from the payout — they never ask you to pay to receive money. Any upfront 'release fee' is a scam, 100% of the time.

patterns.name: Phishing / smishing (fake bank or SARS messages)
patterns.description: Messages impersonating banks, SARS, or courier companies with urgent links to 'verify' or 'unlock' your account. The link harvests your login and card details.
patterns.sa_example: 'SARS: You have a tax refund of R8 450. Click here to claim.' SARS never sends refund links by SMS — refunds are processed inside official eFiling.
patterns.advice: Never click links in unsolicited SMS/WhatsApp/email about money. Open your banking app or type the official web address yourself. Banks and SARS never ask for your PIN, password, or OTP.

patterns.name: Vishing — fake bank fraud department
patterns.description: A caller claims to be from your bank's fraud department and pressures you to read out an OTP 'to stop a fraudulent transaction'. The OTP actually authorises THEIR transaction.
patterns.sa_example: Caller ID spoofed to look like your bank: 'We detected fraud — read us the OTP we just sent so we can block it.'
patterns.advice: A bank will NEVER ask for an OTP, PIN, or password — the OTP is the criminal's key. Hang up and call the number on the back of your card.

patterns.name: WhatsApp / Telegram 'investment' groups
patterns.description: Group chats full of fake members posting 'profit screenshots' and 'withdrawal proofs', run by a 'mentor' or 'account manager' who takes deposits and vanishes.
patterns.sa_example: 'Forex mentor' groups targeting stokvel members and church groups with screenshots of luxury cars and fake withdrawal receipts.
patterns.advice: Screenshots prove nothing — they are trivial to fake. Real financial advisors are FSCA-licensed and do not recruit in WhatsApp groups. Never hand money to an 'account manager' found on social media.

patterns.name: Pig-butchering / fake crypto platform
patterns.description: A fake trading platform shows your 'balance' growing, but every withdrawal attempt demands another deposit — 'tax', 'fees', 'unfreeze'. The balance is fiction; only your deposits are real.
patterns.sa_example: Victims 'invest' R5 000, watch the app show R40 000, then pay R8 000 'tax' to withdraw — and are told to pay again. This pattern is exploding in SA.
patterns.advice: If you must PAY to withdraw YOUR money, it is a scam — full stop. Legitimate platforms deduct fees from the balance. Report to the FSCA and SAPS immediately; do not send 'one last payment'.

patterns.name: Romance scam
patterns.description: An online relationship (never met in person, always an excuse not to video call) that escalates to emergencies requiring money — medical bills, customs fees, plane tickets.
patterns.sa_example: 'Engineer on an oil rig' romances a victim for months, then needs R15 000 for 'customs' to ship a 'gift package'.
patterns.advice: Never send money, gift cards, or crypto to someone you have not met in person. Reverse-image-search their photos. Talk to a trusted friend before sending anything — shame is the scammer's best tool.

patterns.name: Job / recruitment scam
patterns.description: Fake job offers that require you to PAY first — for training, uniforms, background checks, or 'registration'. Real employers pay you; you never pay them.
patterns.sa_example: 'Learnership' WhatsApp messages asking R350 'registration' for a guaranteed Transnet/Eskom/mine job. These employers never recruit via WhatsApp.
patterns.advice: Any job that asks for money upfront is fake — this is the single rule. Apply only through official company career portals. Verify 'learnerships' with the company directly.

patterns.name: Loan scam / illegal upfront loan fees
patterns.description: 'Guaranteed loans' for blacklisted borrowers that demand an 'admin' or 'insurance' fee before payout. Charging upfront fees for credit is illegal in South Africa.
patterns.sa_example: SMS: 'R100 000 loan approved, blacklisted welcome. Pay R500 admin fee to release.' The NCA makes upfront loan fees illegal.
patterns.advice: Under the National Credit Act, upfront fees before a loan payout are illegal — that alone proves the scam. Borrow only from NCR-registered credit providers; check registration at ncr.org.za.

patterns.name: Marketplace / goods non-delivery scam
patterns.description: Goods (cars, puppies, electronics, rentals) advertised below market price with pressure to pay a deposit before viewing. The goods do not exist.
patterns.sa_example: A 'bakkie' on Facebook Marketplace at half its value — 'pay R5 000 deposit, other buyers are waiting'. The photos are stolen from a real listing.
patterns.advice: Never pay before seeing the item in person. Below-market price + urgency + deposit-before-viewing = scam. For cars, verify registration and VIN; meet at a police station safe-trade zone.

patterns.name: Stokvel / savings-club fraud
patterns.description: Fake or hijacked savings clubs where the 'treasurer' disappears with the pooled money, or pyramid schemes dressed in stokvel language to exploit trust.
patterns.sa_example: Fake 'grocery stokvels' on WhatsApp each December, and pyramid schemes calling themselves 'stokvels' where earnings depend on recruiting new members.
patterns.advice: A real stokvel pays out members' own contributions in rotation — it cannot multiply money. If a 'stokvel' promises growth or needs recruits, it is a pyramid. Keep written constitutions, signatories, and bank-issued statements.

patterns.name: Authority impersonation (police / SARS / court)
patterns.description: Calls or messages claiming you face arrest, fines, or an audit unless you pay immediately — often by EFT, voucher, or crypto. Authorities never collect fines this way.
patterns.sa_example: 'This is Sergeant X, a warrant is out for your arrest — pay the admission-of-guilt fine now by EFT.' SAPS never takes payment by phone.
patterns.advice: Real fines are paid through official channels (court, AARTO, SARS eFiling) — never via a phone call. Hang up, look up the official number yourself, and verify.
